section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: One app, a billion users, five very different kinds of data
body: The book's running example is a global app with 1 billion users. It stores five kinds of data: profiles (small structured records, billions of them, read very often), photos and videos (large binary blobs, petabytes to exabytes, written once and read many times), messages (small records, very write-heavy), logs and events (every click and server action, append-only and huge), and analytics and ML data (a data lake of columnar files read in large scans). Each kind has a different shape, so no single storage system fits all of them.
deeper:
The point of the example is that access pattern, not just size, drives design. Profiles are read far more often than written, so read latency and caching dominate. Photos and videos are immutable once written, which makes cheap bulk media and erasure coding attractive, but they start hot and cool down over time. Messages flip the ratio: writes arrive constantly, so write throughput and per-user ordering matter most. Logs and events are append-only streams whose main requirements are append throughput and cheap retention. Analytics and ML data is read by batch jobs and model training in large sequential scans, so aggregate throughput beats per-request latency.

The chapter ends by mapping each of these to a storage interface and medium: profiles to replicated databases or key-value stores with a cache, photos to object stores, messages to log-structured (LSM) databases, logs to a log system like Kafka landing in a DFS or object store, and analytics to a data lake. The rest of the book keeps returning to this app, so it is worth remembering the five shapes.

quiz.q: Why can't one storage system serve profiles, photos and messages equally well?
quiz.a: Their access patterns conflict: profiles are read-heavy small records needing low latency, photos are huge write-once blobs needing cheap durability, and messages are write-heavy needing high write throughput and ordering.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: 13 dead drives a day: at scale, failure is the normal case
body: At big-tech scale, hardware failure is routine, not exceptional. Backblaze runs about 301,000 data drives and measured an annualized failure rate (AFR), the fraction of drives that die per year, of 1.57% across its fleet in 2024. That is roughly 4,700 dead drives per year, or about 13 per day, and Backblaze is much smaller than Google or Meta. So software, not humans, must detect disk death and repair the lost data automatically.
deeper:
The Google File System paper said the same thing back in 2003: "component failures are the norm rather than the exception." That sentence shaped a generation of storage design. If a human had to respond to every dead drive, a large fleet would need people swapping disks and triggering rebuilds around the clock, and every delay would leave some data with fewer copies than intended.

The practical consequences run through the whole book. Data must be stored redundantly (replication or erasure coding) so a single loss never loses bytes. The system must notice a failure on its own, decide when to rebuild (GFS waited 15 minutes, because most node unavailability is short), and re-create missing copies elsewhere. Placement must spread copies so one event cannot kill all of them.

The same 1.57% AFR also feeds the chapter's back-of-envelope durability math, where it shows that independent failures alone would give nearly ten nines, and why correlated failures make reality worse.

quiz.q: Why does a 1.57% annual failure rate force automated repair at large companies?
quiz.a: Across hundreds of thousands of drives, 1.57% means about 13 failures every day. Humans cannot keep up, so software must detect failures and rebuild data automatically.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: Metadata, the list of where things live, becomes its own database
body: Metadata is data about data: names, sizes, and where each piece physically lives. On a laptop it is trivial. At scale it is not. If each of 1 billion users stores ten photos, that is ten billion objects, and simply keeping the list of where each one lives becomes a large distributed database in its own right. Chapter 2 argues that scaling metadata is the central problem of distributed file systems.
deeper:
Every read starts with a metadata lookup: before you can fetch a photo's bytes, something must tell you which machines hold them. That makes metadata both hot (touched on every operation) and critical (lose it and the data is effectively gone, even if the bytes survive).

The chapter gives one concrete example of keeping metadata in memory: the HDFS NameNode keeps the whole file system namespace in DRAM. That is fast, but it caps the namespace at what one machine's memory can hold, the kind of limit that becomes a problem at billions of objects.

The block/file/object comparison in this chapter also reflects metadata cost. File storage's scale limit is listed as "metadata server scaling", because hierarchical directories, rename and listing need a coordinated namespace. Object storage uses a flat namespace of buckets and keys, which is easier to spread across many machines, so its scale limit is "very high". Chapter 2 walks through how GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic and others attacked this problem.

quiz.q: Why does metadata become a scaling problem even though each record is tiny?
quiz.a: Billions of objects means billions of location records, each touched on every access. Keeping that list fast, consistent and durable requires a large distributed database of its own.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: Disk arms, flash wear, and the speed of light don't negotiate
body: Storage design runs into physics. A hard disk's arm moves at about the same speed it did twenty years ago, yet disks now hold far more data, so each terabyte gets less random access. Flash cells wear out after a limited number of writes. Light takes real time to cross an ocean, which limits how fast data can be replicated between continents. Good storage designs accept these limits and are built around them rather than hoping they go away.
deeper:
Each of these limits gets its own treatment later in the chapter. The disk arm problem becomes the IOPS-per-TB problem: a 7,200 RPM drive does roughly 80 random IOPS whether it holds 4 TB or 30 TB, so IOPS per TB falls from 20 to about 2.7. Meta's Haystack photo store hit this wall and had to buy extra drives only for IOPS.

Flash wear shows up as program/erase (P/E) cycle limits. Denser cells (QLC, 4 bits per cell) are cheaper but wear faster than TLC (3 bits). Write amplification from garbage collection multiplies the flash writes behind each application write, burning through that budget faster.

The speed of light matters for multi-region placement: spreading copies across regions protects against the largest failure domains (natural disasters, regional control-plane bugs), but every synchronous cross-ocean write pays the travel time. The lesson is to know which physical limit your design is up against and let it shape the architecture.

quiz.q: Why is "a faster disk arm" not the fix for HDD random-access limits?
quiz.a: Arm and spindle speeds have barely improved in 20 years; it is a mechanical limit. Designers instead move hot data to flash and give HDDs large sequential I/O.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: 3 copies vs 1.33: why storage efficiency is a billion-dollar question
body: At scale, cost dominates storage decisions. Keeping each byte 3 times (3x replication) versus 1.33 times (an efficient erasure code) means buying 3 exabytes of disk instead of 1.33 exabytes for every exabyte of user data. Microsoft said erasure coding could cut its storage cost by "over 50%" and its datacenter footprint "by 1/2". Small differences in overhead become enormous amounts of hardware, power and floor space.
deeper:
The gap between 3x and 1.33x is not a rounding error: it is 1.67 extra exabytes of raw disk per exabyte stored, plus the servers, racks, power and cooling to run it. That is why the chapter spends so much time on erasure coding and on Azure's Local Reconstruction Codes, which reach 1.33x while keeping repair cheap. Even the last step matters: going from RS(6,3) at 1.5x to LRC at 1.33x saves 0.17x, which on one exabyte is 170 petabytes of disk you do not buy.

Cost also hides in less obvious places. The chapter's common mistake is comparing SSD and HDD only on cost per GB: for hot data, the real limit is often IOPS per dollar, and buying cheap disks just for IOPS wastes their capacity. Haystack's effective replication factor rose from 3.6x to 5.3x for exactly this reason. The senior staff lens frames it as cost per useful byte per month, not raw price per GB.

quiz.q: Why is the jump from 3x replication to 1.33x erasure coding so significant at big-tech scale?
quiz.a: Overhead multiplies all raw hardware. Per exabyte of user data it saves about 1.67 exabytes of disk, plus servers, power and space; Microsoft cited over 50% cost savings.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
title: The four questions every storage design review should start with
body: Senior staff lens: in any storage design review, ask four questions first. What is the data type and access pattern? What is the durability target? What is the latency target, including the tail such as p99 (the latency the slowest 1% of requests exceed)? What does it cost per useful byte per month? Most bad storage designs fail one of these basic questions, not a clever algorithm question.
deeper:
Each question maps to a major theme of the chapter. Data type and access pattern decide the interface (block, file or object) and the medium: small, hot, mutable data wants flash with replication; large, cold, immutable data wants HDD with erasure coding.

The durability target decides redundancy and placement. Eleven nines of durability, as S3 is designed for, is not achieved by copy count alone: correlated failures mean copies must be spread across racks, power domains and zones.

The latency target must include the tail. SSD garbage collection makes p99 and p99.9 far worse than the median, and a request that fans out to 100 devices is likely to hit at least one slow one. Designs that only quote median latency hide this.

Cost per useful byte captures overhead (3x replication vs 1.33x erasure coding), wasted capacity bought only for IOPS, and media price. Asking these four up front catches most mismatches before anyone debates algorithms.

quiz.q: Why does the senior staff lens ask about cost per useful byte rather than cost per raw GB?
quiz.a: Raw price ignores redundancy overhead and capacity bought only for IOPS. What matters is what you pay for each byte of actual user data stored and served.

title: The media ladder: every step down is slower, cheaper, bigger
body: All storage is built from physical media arranged on a speed-versus-cost ladder. From fastest and most expensive to slowest and cheapest: DRAM (nanoseconds, volatile), persistent memory (Intel Optane, discontinued 2022), NVMe SSD (tens of microseconds, gigabytes per second), SATA SSD (same flash behind a slower interface), HDD (milliseconds, cheapest online media), and tape (seconds to minutes, cheapest per GB, offline). Systems mix these tiers, putting hot data high and bulk data low.
deeper:
The ratios are what to remember, not exact figures. DRAM is about 1,000 times faster than NVMe for a random read, and NVMe is about 100 times faster than HDD. Across the whole ladder, latency spans about six orders of magnitude, from roughly 100 ns for DRAM to roughly 10 ms for an HDD random read, and seconds or more for tape.

"Online" versus "offline" is a key divide. HDD is the cheapest medium that can answer a request immediately. Tape needs a robot to load and wind a cartridge, so it only fits data you keep forever and almost never read.

Volatility is another divide: DRAM loses everything on power loss, so it serves as cache and hot metadata, never as the only copy of durable data. Persistent memory tried to be both fast and non-volatile but lost commercially.

Real systems use several rungs at once. Google's Colossus, for example, keeps bulk data on HDD and uses an SSD cache with machine learning to place the hottest data on flash.

quiz.q: Why do large systems combine several media tiers instead of picking the single best one?
quiz.a: No medium is both fast and cheap. Mixing tiers lets hot data get fast media while bulk data sits on cheap media, balancing latency against cost per GB.

title: DRAM: 100 nanoseconds, gone when the power goes
body: DRAM (dynamic RAM) is a computer's main memory. A memory reference takes about 100 nanoseconds, making it the fastest medium in the storage hierarchy. It is also volatile: when power is lost, its contents vanish. And it is by far the most expensive medium per GB. Because of this mix of speed, cost and volatility, large systems use DRAM for caches and for hot metadata rather than as the durable home of data.
deeper:
The chapter's example is the HDFS NameNode, which keeps the entire file system namespace in RAM. That makes every metadata lookup fast, but it ties namespace size to one machine's memory, a limit Chapter 2 explores.

DRAM's price per GB is listed as the highest of any medium and varies a lot with the memory market. That is why DRAM caches (Chapter 6) hold only the hottest data, such as profile records in the running example, while the durable copy lives on SSD.

Volatility has a direct consequence for durability. The chapter's example of data that is available but not durable is a value accepted into one server's RAM cache but not yet written to disk: readers can see it right now, but a power loss erases it. Any system that acknowledges writes from DRAM alone is trading durability for speed.

DRAM also sets the bar that other technologies must beat. Intel Optane failed partly because DRAM caches combined with NVMe flash were good enough.

quiz.q: Why is DRAM used for caches and hot metadata but not as the only copy of data?
quiz.a: It is fastest but volatile and most expensive per GB. A power loss erases it, so durable data must live on persistent media, with DRAM holding only hot copies.

title: Intel Optane: a better medium that still lost
body: Persistent memory tried to sit between DRAM and flash: nearly as fast as DRAM, but keeping data after power loss. Intel sold Optane, based on 3D XPoint technology, from 2017. Optane SSDs had about 9 microsecond latency, and Optane DIMMs were about one order of magnitude slower than DRAM. Micron stopped 3D XPoint work in March 2021, and Intel announced the Optane wind-down in July 2022, citing lack of demand.
deeper:
The lesson the chapter draws is strategic, not technical: a technically better medium can still lose if the existing combination is "good enough" and cheaper. Intel cited lack of demand: DRAM caches in front of NVMe flash were good enough for the workloads persistent memory targeted.

In the comparison table, Optane sits between DRAM and NAND on cost per GB, with gigabytes per second of sequential throughput and about 9 microseconds random read latency as an SSD. Compare that with NVMe flash at roughly 50 to 150 microseconds: a real improvement, but not enough to justify a new tier for most buyers.

For senior engineers, Optane is a caution about long-term bets. Building a system that depends on a single-vendor medium creates risk if that medium is discontinued. When evaluating a new technology, ask not only whether it is faster, but whether the gap over cheap, mainstream alternatives is large enough to sustain a market.

quiz.q: Why did Optane fail despite being faster than NAND flash?
quiz.a: DRAM caches plus NVMe flash were good enough and cheaper for most workloads, so demand was too low; Intel wound it down in July 2022.

title: SSDs: NAND flash, no moving parts, microsecond reads
body: A solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in NAND flash chips and has no moving parts. Because there is no arm to move or platter to wait for, random reads take about 50 to 200 microseconds, with NVMe drives at the lower end. That is roughly 100 times faster than a hard disk's random read. SSDs cost more per GB than HDDs, and their flash cells wear out with writes, which shapes how they are used.
deeper:
Late-2025 consumer NVMe SSDs in the 4 to 8 TB range cost roughly $0.05 to $0.10 per GB, compared with $0.014 per GB for HDDs in Backblaze's November 2022 measurement. That price gap is why bulk data still lives on HDD.

The comparison table lists NVMe random read latency as about 50 to 150 microseconds and notes that flash "wears out with writes". Wear is not a side note: each cell survives a limited number of program/erase cycles, and the drive's internal garbage collection adds extra writes (write amplification) that consume that budget faster.

SSDs also look simpler from outside than they are. Flash cannot overwrite a page in place, so firmware called the flash translation layer remaps every write. That hidden machinery explains both SSD wear and occasional latency spikes, covered in the section on how an SSD really works.

Because SSDs deliver far more IOPS per TB than HDDs, the industry puts hot, randomly accessed data on flash.

quiz.q: What fundamental property lets SSDs serve random reads about 100 times faster than HDDs?
quiz.a: No moving parts: there is no seek or rotational wait, so reading any page takes tens of microseconds regardless of where it is.

title: NVMe vs SATA: same flash, very different interface
body: NVMe and SATA SSDs use the same kind of NAND flash; the difference is mostly the interface. SATA's controller interface, AHCI, was designed for hard disks and supports one queue of 32 commands. NVMe runs over PCIe and supports up to 65,535 queues of 65,536 commands each, so many CPU cores can drive the SSD in parallel without contending for one queue. That is why new datacenter flash is almost always NVMe.
deeper:
Bandwidth ceilings differ too. SATA 3 tops out near 600 MB/s. A PCIe 4.0 x4 link has a ceiling near 8 GB/s, and PCIe 5.0 x4 near 16 GB/s. A single SATA link can therefore bottleneck flash that could deliver far more.

AHCI's single 32-command queue made sense for spinning disks, which can only serve one mechanical operation at a time anyway. Flash has many chips that can work in parallel, so a deep, multi-queue interface lets the drive actually use that parallelism. With NVMe, each CPU core can have its own queue, avoiding lock contention in the host.

In the comparison table, SATA SSDs have similar flash latency plus interface overhead, similar cost per GB to NVMe, and "1 queue, 32 commands" in the notes column.

In industry: Meta's 2024 GenAI clusters use high-capacity E1.S NVMe SSDs in their storage servers.

quiz.q: Why can many CPU cores drive an NVMe SSD harder than a SATA SSD with the same flash?
quiz.a: SATA's AHCI has one 32-command queue; NVMe offers up to 65,535 queues of 65,536 commands over PCIe, so cores submit I/O in parallel without contending.

title: HDD random reads cost ~10 ms: seek plus rotation
body: A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data on spinning magnetic platters. To read, a head on an arm moves to the right track (the seek), then waits for the right sector to rotate underneath (rotational latency). At 7,200 RPM, average rotational latency is 4.17 ms. Add a seek of several milliseconds, and a random read costs roughly 10 ms. Sequential reads avoid most of this, so HDDs are fast for streaming but slow for random access.
deeper:
The 4.17 ms figure is half a rotation: at 7,200 revolutions per minute, one turn takes about 8.3 ms, and on average the target sector is half a turn away. The seek varies by distance; the chapter uses about 8 ms as a typical average in its IOPS math.

Sequential reads are a different story. Once the head is on track, data streams off the platter continuously. Enterprise drives in the 2020s can sustain over 500 MB/s with dual-actuator models, and hundreds of MB/s is typical. That is why big HDD-based systems favor large sequential I/O: Dropbox writes 1 GB extents, and Azure seals roughly 1 GB extents before erasure coding them.

HDDs are the cheapest online medium: Backblaze measured about $0.014 per GB in November 2022. But because the mechanical latency has barely changed while capacity grows, each terabyte gets fewer random operations per second every year, which is the IOPS-per-TB problem.

quiz.q: Why are HDDs good at sequential throughput but poor at random reads?
quiz.a: Random reads pay a mechanical seek plus rotational wait (about 10 ms) each time; sequential reads pay it once and then stream data continuously at hundreds of MB/s.

title: SMR: overlapping tracks like roof shingles for 25% more capacity
body: SMR (shingled magnetic recording) packs more data onto a hard disk by overlapping tracks like roof shingles. Seagate's first SMR drives in 2013 gave about 25% more capacity. The catch: you cannot rewrite one track without damaging the next. So the disk is divided into zones that must be written sequentially, like an append-only log. Host-managed SMR makes the software above the drive responsible for respecting these zones.
deeper:
SMR turns a random-write device into something closer to an append-only log. That is fine for systems that already write large immutable extents, and painful for workloads that update small pieces in place.

In industry: Dropbox built its Magic Pocket storage system to write 1 GB extents aligned to 256 MB SMR zones. Because Magic Pocket was designed to write big sequential chunks that fit whole zones, it could respect the SMR zone rules in software. Dropbox expected close to 40% of its data to be on SMR by the end of 2019, with more than 20% overall savings versus its previous design.

The broader lesson is that media quirks are often fine if the software is designed around them. The same pattern shows up with flash, which also cannot overwrite in place: log-structured and append-oriented designs fit both SMR zones and flash erase blocks. The trade-off with host-managed SMR is that the storage software must track zones and write pointers itself instead of relying on the drive to hide the complexity.

quiz.q: Why did Dropbox's Magic Pocket fit host-managed SMR well?
quiz.a: It was built to write large 1 GB extents aligned to 256 MB SMR zones, so its writes were already sequential and append-only within zones, as shingled tracks require.

title: HAMR: a laser heats the platter so bits can shrink
body: HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) uses a tiny laser to heat a spot on the platter while writing, which lets smaller bits be written stably. Smaller bits mean more capacity per drive. Seagate launched its Mozaic 3+ HAMR platform with 28 TB and 30 TB drives in January 2024. HAMR and SMR are the two main tricks keeping hard-disk capacity growing, even though the mechanical speed of the disk has not improved.
deeper:
The capacity trend is steep. Backblaze's fleet added 24 TB drives in December 2024, and HAMR pushes to 30 TB. Backblaze also measured HDD cost falling from $0.114 per GB in 2009 to $0.014 per GB in November 2022, roughly an eightfold drop.

But capacity growth has a downside. A 30 TB HAMR drive still does roughly the same ~80 random IOPS as a 4 TB drive, because its arm and spindle are no faster. In the chapter's table, IOPS per TB falls from 20 at 4 TB to 6.7 at 12 TB, 3.3 at 24 TB, and 2.7 at 30 TB.

So bigger drives make cold, sequentially accessed data cheaper to store while making hot, randomly accessed data harder to serve from HDD. That tension is why industry puts hot data on flash and uses big HDDs for warm and cold data with large sequential I/O. Larger drives also mean more data lost, and more to rebuild, when one fails.

quiz.q: Why do larger HAMR drives make HDDs worse for hot data even as they get cheaper per GB?
quiz.a: Random IOPS per drive stays near 80 while capacity grows, so each TB gets fewer IOPS (2.7 at 30 TB), making random-access workloads IOPS-bound.

title: Tape: cheapest per GB, zero shelf power, minutes to first byte
body: Tape (LTO, Linear Tape-Open) is still used for deep archive. LTO-10 cartridges hold 30 TB or 40 TB native and transfer at 400 MB/s native. Tape is very cheap per GB and uses no power while sitting on a shelf. But a robot must fetch and load the cartridge, then wind the tape to the right spot, so first-byte latency is seconds to minutes. It fits "keep forever, read almost never" data.
deeper:
Tape is the bottom rung of the media ladder: lowest cost per GB and offline. "Offline" means data is not immediately reachable; a mechanical process must happen before any byte is returned. That makes tape unsuitable for anything user-facing but excellent for compliance archives and backups that must be kept for years.

Note the contrast between latency and throughput. First-byte latency is terrible, but once the tape is streaming, 400 MB/s is comparable to a fast hard disk. So tape rewards large, sequential restore jobs and punishes small random reads.

In the running example, backups and compliance archives are rarely read, must be kept for years, and need lowest cost and immutability. The chapter maps them to an archive object tier or tape, with media being an HDD cold tier or tape, covered in Chapters 7 and 11.

The no-power-on-shelf property matters for cost: an idle HDD still spins and draws power, while an idle tape cartridge costs only the shelf space it occupies.

quiz.q: Why is tape a good fit for compliance archives but not for photo serving?
quiz.a: It is cheapest per GB and uses no shelf power, but first-byte latency is seconds to minutes, fine for rarely-read archives, unacceptable for interactive reads.

title: Latency ratios to memorize: DRAM x1,000 NVMe x100 HDD
body: The chapter's comparison table gives rough numbers per medium: DRAM about 100 ns per random read; Optane about 9 microseconds; NVMe SSD about 50 to 150 microseconds; SATA SSD similar flash latency plus interface overhead; a 7,200 RPM HDD about 10 ms; tape seconds to minutes. Treat them as orders of magnitude. The ratios matter more than exact values: DRAM is about 1,000 times faster than NVMe for a random read, and NVMe is about 100 times faster than HDD.
deeper:
The throughput and cost columns tell the rest of the story. DRAM delivers many GB/s at the highest cost per GB, which varies a lot with the memory market. Optane delivered GB/s at a price between DRAM and NAND and was discontinued in 2022. NVMe's interface ceiling is about 8 to 16 GB/s (PCIe 4.0/5.0 x4) at roughly $0.05 to $0.10 per GB for consumer 4 to 8 TB drives in late 2025, and it wears out with writes. SATA SSDs cap near 600 MB/s at similar cost to NVMe, with one queue of 32 commands. HDDs do hundreds of MB/s (over 500 MB/s for some enterprise drives) at $0.014 per GB (Backblaze, November 2022), with IOPS per TB falling. Tape LTO-10 does 400 MB/s native, lowest cost, offline, 30 or 40 TB per cartridge.

Why ratios over exact numbers: prices and generations shift, but the gaps between tiers are stable enough to reason with. If a design needs thousands of random reads per second per TB, the ratios tell you immediately that HDD will not do it.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say to remember the latency ratios rather than exact values?
quiz.a: Exact figures shift with generations and markets, but the order-of-magnitude gaps (DRAM ~1,000x NVMe, NVMe ~100x HDD) stay stable and are what drive design choices.

title: A cheap HDD that can't serve your reads isn't cheap
body: Common mistake: comparing SSD and HDD only on cost per GB. For hot data, the real limit is often IOPS (input/output operations per second) per dollar, not GB per dollar. An HDD does only around 80 random IOPS no matter how big it is. If your workload needs more reads than your disks can serve, you end up buying extra disks just for IOPS and leaving their capacity empty, which destroys the apparent cost advantage.
deeper:
The chapter's real-world example is Meta's Haystack, its old hot-photo store. Because IOPS per drive stayed flat while drive capacity grew, Haystack became IOPS-bound. It bought extra drives purely to get enough IOPS, which pushed its effective replication factor from an ideal 3.6x to 5.3x. In other words, the bytes were stored 5.3 times over, not because durability required it, but because the read rate did.

The right metric depends on the data. For cold, sequentially read data (backups, old photos, analytics scans), cost per GB dominates and HDD wins. For hot, randomly accessed data (profiles, messages, recently uploaded photos), cost per IOPS dominates and flash often wins despite a higher sticker price.

This is why the senior staff lens asks for cost per useful byte per month, and why the industry keeps hot data on flash while mixing IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same HDDs, as Meta's Tectonic does.

quiz.q: Why can a cheaper-per-GB HDD end up more expensive than an SSD for hot data?
quiz.a: Hot data is IOPS-bound. HDDs deliver few IOPS each, so you buy extra drives just for IOPS and leave their capacity empty, raising the real cost per useful byte.

title: Flash can't overwrite: pages are written, whole blocks are erased
body: NAND flash is organized in pages, the unit of read and write (about 2 to 16 KB), grouped into blocks, the unit of erase (about 128 to 256 pages). You cannot overwrite a page in place. A page must be erased first, and erase only works on a whole block at once. So an "update" on an SSD actually writes the new data to a fresh page and marks the old page stale.
deeper:
The mismatch between write unit and erase unit is the root of most SSD behavior. If a block holds 256 pages and you want to change one, erasing the whole block would destroy 255 pages of valid data. So the drive never updates in place; it writes somewhere new and remembers that the old copy is garbage.

That creates three consequences explored in the rest of the section. First, something must track where each logical piece of data currently lives: that is the flash translation layer. Second, stale pages accumulate, so the drive must eventually reclaim them by copying valid pages out of a block and erasing it: garbage collection. Third, those copies are extra writes the host never requested, measured as write amplification, which both wears out cells faster and competes with foreground I/O.

The no-overwrite rule is also why append-oriented, log-structured designs fit flash well: they naturally write new data sequentially instead of updating in place.

quiz.q: Why can't an SSD simply update a page in place when data changes?
quiz.a: Flash pages must be erased before rewriting, and erase works only on whole blocks of 128-256 pages; erasing a block would destroy other valid pages, so updates go to fresh pages.

title: The FTL: firmware that makes flash look like a normal disk
body: The flash translation layer (FTL) is firmware inside an SSD. It maps logical block addresses, the addresses the operating system sees, to physical pages, where the data really sits in flash. Every time the host overwrites a logical address, the FTL writes the data to a fresh physical page and updates the mapping. This hidden remapping is why an SSD looks like an ordinary rewritable disk from the outside, despite flash's no-overwrite rule.
deeper:
The FTL is the SSD's own little storage system. Beyond address mapping, it runs garbage collection (reclaiming blocks full of stale pages) and wear leveling (spreading program/erase cycles evenly so no block wears out early).

Because the FTL hides all this, the host cannot directly see when the drive is busy doing internal work. A read might land on a chip that is in the middle of erasing a block, and it simply waits. From outside, that shows up as a random latency spike, which is why SSD tail latency can be much worse than the median.

The FTL's abstraction is convenient but not free. Its behavior depends on how full the drive is, how much spare over-provisioned capacity it has, and what the write pattern looks like. Small random overwrites on a nearly full drive force the FTL to do the most copying. That is why the senior staff lens insists on benchmarking drives that are 80% full and written to steady state: fresh-out-of-box drives have not yet made the FTL work hard.

quiz.q: Why does an SSD appear to support in-place overwrites even though flash does not?
quiz.a: The FTL remaps each logical address to a new physical page on every write and marks the old page stale, hiding the no-overwrite rule from the host.

title: Garbage collection: the SSD writes you never asked for
body: Over time, flash blocks fill with a mix of valid pages and stale ones left behind by updates. To create free blocks for new writes, the SSD runs garbage collection (GC): it copies the still-valid pages from a block to somewhere else, then erases the whole block. Those copies are writes the host never asked for. GC is necessary because of flash's no-overwrite rule, but it costs extra flash writes and competes with normal I/O.
deeper:
How much GC costs depends on how many valid pages each victim block holds. If a block is mostly stale, GC copies little and frees a lot. If a block is mostly valid, GC copies nearly the whole block to free a few pages, which is expensive.

Two factors shape this. A nearly full drive has fewer free blocks, so GC must pick victims that still hold many valid pages. Small random overwrites scatter stale pages across many blocks instead of freeing whole blocks at once. Large sequential writes, by contrast, tend to invalidate whole blocks together, leaving GC little to copy.

GC has two visible effects. It multiplies total flash writes, measured as the write amplification factor, which consumes the cells' limited program/erase cycles and shortens drive life. And because GC reads, writes and erases on the same flash chips your application uses, it causes latency spikes: a read that lands on a chip busy erasing must wait. Both effects follow from the same mechanism.

quiz.q: What two costs does SSD garbage collection impose, and why?
quiz.a: Extra flash writes (copying valid pages) wear cells faster, and GC work occupies the same chips as foreground I/O, causing latency spikes.

title: Write amplification: 1 GB from your app, 3 GB into flash
body: The write amplification factor (WAF) measures SSD overhead: WAF = bytes written to flash divided by bytes written by the host. A WAF of 3 means each 1 GB your application writes costs 3 GB of flash writes, because garbage collection copies valid pages behind the scenes. Small random overwrites on a nearly full drive give the worst WAF. Large sequential writes give the best. WAF matters because it drives both drive lifetime and latency.
deeper:
Over-provisioning is the main hardware lever for lowering WAF. It means keeping some flash capacity hidden from the host as spare. With more spare room, GC can wait until blocks hold fewer valid pages before reclaiming them, so each GC pass copies less data.

The software lever is write pattern. Writing large sequential chunks tends to invalidate whole blocks together, keeping WAF near its minimum. Scattering small random overwrites across a full drive is the worst case, because every block ends up partly valid.

High WAF is also a lifetime cost. Drives are rated in TBW (terabytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day), and those budgets count flash writes, not host writes. A WAF of 3 uses up the endurance three times faster than the application's own write volume suggests.

Finally, the extra GC writes occupy flash chips, so high WAF usually comes with worse tail latency. This is why the chapter's quiz asks why WAF affects both lifetime and the p99.

quiz.q: Why does high write amplification hurt both SSD lifetime and tail latency?
quiz.a: Extra GC writes consume limited program/erase cycles faster, shortening life, and GC activity competes with foreground reads on the same chips, causing p99 spikes.

title: QLC is cheaper, TLC lasts longer: flash wears out
body: Each flash cell survives only a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles before it wears out. Storing more bits per cell is cheaper but wears faster: QLC (4 bits per cell) has lower endurance than TLC (3 bits per cell). The flash translation layer does wear leveling, spreading P/E cycles evenly across blocks so no area dies early. Drives are rated in TBW (terabytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day).
deeper:
Endurance ratings count writes to flash, so write amplification directly shortens a drive's usable life. If an application writes 1 TB per day and the WAF is 3, the drive absorbs 3 TB of flash writes daily. A drive rated for a certain TBW reaches that limit three times sooner than a naive estimate. The chapter's summary: high WAF is also a lifetime cost.

The QLC versus TLC choice is a classic cost trade-off. QLC's extra bit per cell lowers price per GB, which suits read-mostly or cold data on flash. TLC's higher endurance suits write-heavy workloads such as the running example's messages, which are small records written constantly.

Wear leveling matters because workloads are uneven. Without it, a few hot logical addresses would hammer the same physical blocks until they failed while most of the drive stayed fresh. By remapping writes across all blocks, the FTL makes the whole drive age together.

The comparison table sums it up in one note for NVMe SSDs: "wears out with writes."

quiz.q: When would you choose TLC over cheaper QLC flash?
quiz.a: For write-heavy workloads: TLC's higher P/E endurance lasts longer under heavy writes (amplified by WAF), while QLC suits read-mostly data where cost per GB matters more.

title: Why SSD p99 looks bad even when the median looks great
body: SSD garbage collection competes with your I/O for the same flash chips. Most reads take about 100 microseconds, but a read that lands on a chip busy erasing a block must wait much longer. The median looks great, while the p99 or p99.9 (the slowest 1% or 0.1% of requests) looks bad. These slow outliers are called tail latency, and they are a direct side effect of the SSD's hidden internal work.
deeper:
Tail latency matters more at scale because of fan-out. If one user request reads from 100 devices in parallel, it must wait for the slowest one. Even if each device is slow only rarely, the chance that at least one of the 100 is slow becomes high, so the request's latency tracks the devices' tail, not their median.

Systems fight this in two ways. Hedged reads send a backup request if the first one is slow and take whichever returns first. Or, with erasure coding, the system can reconstruct the needed data from other fragments instead of waiting for the slow one.

In industry: Azure Storage does the second. If a fragment read looks slow, it starts a reconstruction from other fragments in parallel and returns whichever finishes first.

The tail also depends on drive state. A nearly full drive under mixed reads and writes does more GC than a fresh one, so benchmark results on new, empty drives understate the problem.

quiz.q: Why does SSD tail latency matter more when a request fans out to many devices?
quiz.a: The request waits for the slowest device; with 100 devices, at least one being in a GC stall is likely, so overall latency follows the tail, not the median.

title: Benchmark the p99.9 on a full, steady-state drive
body: Senior staff lens: design for the tail, not the median. When someone shows you an SSD benchmark, ask for p99.9 latency (the latency only 0.1% of requests exceed) under mixed read and write load, on a drive that is 80% full and has been written to steady state. Fresh-out-of-box benchmarks hide garbage collection entirely, because a new, empty drive has plenty of free blocks and no need to copy valid pages.
deeper:
Each condition in that request targets a specific way benchmarks mislead. Mixed read/write load matters because GC is triggered by writes; a read-only test never forces the drive to reclaim blocks, so reads never collide with erases. The 80% full condition matters because a nearly full drive has fewer free blocks and must reclaim blocks that still hold many valid pages, raising write amplification. Steady state matters because a drive's first pass through its capacity writes into clean blocks; only after the whole drive has been written, and overwritten, does GC run continuously.

Asking for p99.9 rather than median or average matters because at scale requests fan out. With many devices per request, the rare slow device determines user-visible latency. Averages can look excellent while the tail is terrible.

The same principle applies beyond SSDs. The chapter's four review questions explicitly include "the latency target, including the tail, like p99", and notes that problems in the bottom storage layer, like tail latency, show up in every layer above.

quiz.q: Why are fresh-out-of-box SSD benchmarks misleading?
quiz.a: An empty new drive has free blocks, so garbage collection never runs. Real drives that are full and in steady state do constant GC, which inflates tail latency.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
title: ~80 random IOPS per HDD, and it hasn't changed in 20 years
body: One random hard-disk I/O costs about one seek plus half a rotation. Assume 7,200 RPM, giving 4.17 ms average rotational latency, and an average seek of about 8 ms (a typical figure, not from one datasheet). That is about 12 ms per I/O, or roughly 80 random IOPS (I/O operations per second) per drive. This number barely changed in 20 years, because disk arms and spindles did not get faster. Capacity, however, did.
deeper:
The arithmetic is simple: 1 second divided by about 12 ms per operation is about 83, rounded to 80. Nothing in that formula depends on how many bytes the drive holds. A bigger platter or denser recording (SMR, HAMR) packs more data under the same head, but the head still moves and the platter still spins at the same speeds.

Contrast this with sequential throughput, which does grow with density: modern enterprise drives can sustain hundreds of MB/s and over 500 MB/s for dual-actuator models, because more bits pass under the head per rotation.

The practical rule is that HDDs are sized by capacity but hot workloads are sized by IOPS. If a workload needs 800 random reads per second, it needs about 10 drives' worth of spindles, regardless of whether it fills 4 TB or 400 TB. This mismatch is the root of the IOPS-per-TB problem and why the industry moved hot data to flash.

quiz.q: Why doesn't a bigger hard drive deliver more random IOPS?
quiz.a: Random IOPS are set by seek time and rotation speed (about 12 ms per I/O), which are mechanical and unchanged; added capacity only puts more data under the same slow head.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
title: IOPS per TB: from 20 at 4 TB down to 2.7 at 30 TB
body: If every hard drive does about 80 random IOPS, then IOPS per terabyte falls as drives grow: a 4 TB drive gives 20 IOPS per TB, 12 TB gives 6.7, 24 TB gives 3.3, and a 30 TB HAMR drive gives 2.7. Meta's Tectonic paper states it directly: because IOPS per hard drive has stayed steady as density increased, IOPS per terabyte of storage has declined over time. Bigger drives store data cheaper but serve it slower.
deeper:
This is the key economic tension of HDD storage. Every generation lowers cost per GB (Backblaze saw $0.114 per GB in 2009 fall to $0.014 in November 2022) but also lowers the access rate each stored byte can receive. Data that was hot enough for 4 TB drives may be too hot for 24 TB drives.

The decline pushes design in three directions the chapter names. First, hot data moves to flash, which delivers vastly more IOPS per TB. Second, big HDDs are reserved for warm and cold data read with large sequential I/O, where throughput still scales. Third, systems mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, so one workload uses the spare IOPS and another uses the spare space. Meta's Tectonic does exactly this, covered in Chapter 2.

Without those strategies, operators end up buying drives for IOPS and leaving capacity empty, which is what happened to Meta's Haystack.

quiz.q: Why does IOPS per TB keep falling for hard drives?
quiz.a: Random IOPS per drive stays around 80 because mechanics don't improve, while capacity keeps rising, so each terabyte gets a shrinking share of the same IOPS.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
title: Haystack: when buying disks for IOPS pushed 3.6x to 5.3x
body: In industry: Meta's old hot-photo store, Haystack, became IOPS-bound. As drives grew, the photos stored on each drive demanded more random reads than the drive's roughly 80 IOPS could deliver. To keep up, Meta bought extra drives just for their IOPS. That pushed Haystack's effective replication factor, the raw storage used per byte of data, from an ideal 3.6x to 5.3x, according to Meta's Tectonic paper.
deeper:
The effective replication factor rose not because durability needed more copies, but because the read rate did. Extra drives were added for spindles, and their capacity largely went unused. In cost terms, Meta paid for roughly 5.3 bytes of raw disk per byte of photos instead of 3.6.

Haystack is the chapter's clearest example of the common mistake of comparing media only on cost per GB. For hot data, cost per IOPS is often the real constraint, and a cheap-per-GB HDD that cannot serve the read rate is not cheap.

Meta's later shared storage layer, Tectonic (described in 2021), mixes IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, so the spare capacity left by hot workloads can be used by cold ones. Moving Meta's data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut its number of warehouse clusters by 10x. The same pressure explains why the industry generally puts hot data on flash and keeps big HDDs for warm and cold data.

quiz.q: What made Haystack's effective replication factor rise from 3.6x to 5.3x?
quiz.a: Haystack was IOPS-bound: HDD IOPS per TB kept falling, so Meta bought extra drives just to get enough random reads, adding raw capacity that stored no extra copies.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
title: Flash for hot, HDD for bulk: how the industry escapes IOPS limits
body: Because HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling, the industry uses three strategies. It puts hot, randomly accessed data on flash. It keeps big hard drives for warm and cold data read with large sequential I/O. And it mixes IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks so both resources get used, as Meta's Tectonic does. Google's Colossus adds an SSD cache called L4 and uses machine learning to place the hottest data on SSD.
deeper:
Each strategy tackles the imbalance from a different angle. Flash solves hot data outright: NVMe SSDs serve random reads in tens of microseconds with deep parallel queues, so IOPS stop being the bottleneck. The price is higher cost per GB, acceptable only for the fraction of data that is actually hot.

Large sequential I/O plays to HDD strengths. Streaming reads avoid repeated seeks, so throughput scales with density even when IOPS do not. Dropbox writes 1 GB extents aligned to SMR zones, and Azure seals extents at about 1 GB, both favoring large sequential I/O.

Tenant mixing is a scheduling fix: a single cluster that stores both hot blobs and cold warehouse data can spend the disks' IOPS on the former and their capacity on the latter.

In industry: Colossus's L4 SSD cache, described by Google in March 2025, lets bulk data stay on HDD while machine learning predicts which data is hot enough to deserve flash. It is the same pattern the chapter summarizes: hot data on flash, cold data on HDD.

quiz.q: How does mixing IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks help?
quiz.a: Hot tenants use the disks' limited IOPS while cold tenants fill their spare capacity, so neither resource sits idle and fewer drives are bought just for IOPS.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
title: Block storage: numbered blocks, no names, no meaning
body: Storage is also defined by its interface, meaning how a program asks for data. Block storage exposes a raw device: an array of fixed-size blocks (for example 4 KB) addressed by number, with no names. A file system or database running on top decides what the blocks mean. Examples include local NVMe drives, AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk and Ceph RBD. Block storage is used mainly for databases and virtual machine disks.
deeper:
Block is the lowest-level of the three interfaces. It supports updating any block in place, has no namespace at all (just addresses), and typically offers the lowest latency. Its scale limit is one volume: a block device belongs to one file system or database at a time, so it does not naturally scale out to a shared namespace across many machines.

That simplicity is exactly why databases and VMs like it. A database engine wants full control over layout, caching and write ordering, and block storage gets out of its way. A VM wants a virtual disk that looks like a real one so the guest operating system can run its own file system.

Network block devices such as AWS EBS and Google Persistent Disk provide that same raw-device abstraction over the network, backed by a distributed storage layer. Chapter 4 covers block, local and Kubernetes storage in depth, including local NVMe, CSI and persistent volumes. The chapter's takeaway: block dominates databases and VMs.

quiz.q: Why do databases and VMs prefer block storage over file or object storage?
quiz.a: Block gives a raw, lowest-latency device with in-place updates and no imposed structure, letting the database or guest OS control layout and semantics itself.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
title: File storage and POSIX: familiar semantics, costly to distribute
body: File storage exposes directories and files with operations like open, read, write, rename and list. POSIX is the standard set of file semantics, such as atomic rename and byte-range writes. Full POSIX is expensive to provide across many machines, so large distributed file systems often relax it. File storage is used for HPC and AI training (Lustre, GPFS), shared home directories, and Hadoop (HDFS).
deeper:
File storage sits between block and object. It supports in-place updates of byte ranges, uses a hierarchical namespace of directories, and typically has low to medium latency. Its scale limit is metadata server scaling: every open, rename and directory listing needs a consistent view of the directory tree, and that metadata must be coordinated.

That is why POSIX is costly to distribute. An atomic rename of a directory, for example, must appear instantaneous to every client, which requires coordination across whatever machines hold the metadata. Many big systems therefore relax some guarantees. GFS, for instance, offered a record append with a relaxed consistency model that can even show duplicates.

Chapter 2 is devoted to distributed file systems (GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph, Lustre) and argues that scaling metadata is their central problem. The chapter's takeaway: file dominates HPC, AI training, and legacy big-data workloads.

quiz.q: Why do big distributed file systems often relax full POSIX semantics?
quiz.a: POSIX guarantees like atomic rename and consistent directory views require coordinating metadata across machines, which is expensive and limits scale.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
title: Object storage: flat keys, whole objects, no in-place update
body: Object storage exposes a flat namespace of buckets and keys. You PUT, GET (the whole object or a byte range) and DELETE whole objects. There is usually no in-place update and no real rename. Examples include Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob and Ceph RGW. Object storage is the default home for large, write-once data such as photos, backups, logs and data lakes.
deeper:
Giving up in-place updates and hierarchy is what lets object storage scale. A flat namespace of keys is easy to partition across many machines, so there is no single metadata tree to coordinate. Prefixes in keys look like folders to users, but they are just part of the key string, which is why "renaming a folder" is not a cheap operation.

The trade-off is latency and semantics. Object stores are typically accessed over HTTP with tens of milliseconds of latency, and updating one byte means replacing the whole object. That rules them out as the direct backing for databases, but it fits immutable data perfectly: a photo is written once and read many times, never edited in place.

In the running example, photos and videos go to an object or blob store (replicated when new, erasure coded when warm), and logs and analytics data often land in an object store too. Chapter 3 covers how S3, GCS and Azure Blob are built. The chapter's takeaway: object storage dominates large, immutable data.

quiz.q: Why does object storage scale better than file storage?
quiz.a: Its flat key namespace with whole-object operations avoids a coordinated directory tree, rename and in-place updates, so metadata partitions easily across machines.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
title: Block vs file vs object: one table to rule the trade-offs
body: The three storage interfaces differ on six points. Unit: fixed-size block, file in a directory tree, or whole object with a key. Update in place: block yes, file yes (byte ranges), object no. Namespace: none, hierarchical, or flat. Typical latency: lowest, low to medium, or medium (tens of ms over HTTP). Scale limit: one volume, metadata server scaling, or very high. Typical users: databases and VMs; HPC, AI training and Hadoop; media, backups and lakes.
deeper:
Read the table as a spectrum. Moving from block to object, you give up in-place updates and some latency, and gain scale (file is the only one with a hierarchy). Block is fastest and most flexible but bounded by one volume. File adds a shared hierarchical namespace, but that namespace is exactly what becomes the scaling bottleneck. Object removes hierarchy and in-place update and scales very high as a result.

Choosing the interface is really choosing which semantics your application needs. A database needs in-place updates and low latency, so block. An AI training job needs many readers to share a familiar directory tree, so file (Lustre, GPFS). A photo service needs to store billions of immutable blobs cheaply, so object.

The chapter's summary: object storage dominates large, immutable data; block dominates databases and VMs; file dominates HPC, AI training and legacy big data. The lines are blurring, though, as object stores add file-like features.

quiz.q: What does object storage give up compared with block storage, and what does it gain?
quiz.a: It gives up in-place updates and the lowest latency; it gains named objects in a flat, easily partitioned key namespace (block has no names at all) that scales very high.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
title: Google Rapid Storage: when object storage starts acting like files
body: In industry: the line between file and object storage is blurring. Google's 2025 Rapid Storage for Cloud Storage offers sub-millisecond latency, unlimited appends, and a hierarchical namespace, all built on Colossus's stateful protocol. Those are traits traditionally associated with file systems or block devices, not object stores, which usually have tens of milliseconds of latency, no in-place updates, and a flat namespace.
deeper:
Compare Rapid Storage's features against the chapter's interface table. Typical object latency is "medium (tens of ms typical over HTTP)", and the namespace is "flat (prefixes look like folders)". Rapid Storage offers sub-millisecond latency and a hierarchical namespace, and supports unlimited appends rather than only whole-object replacement.

The key enabler is the storage layer underneath. Colossus underpins most Google Cloud products and is used by Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. Because Google already has one shared, durable storage layer, it can expose different interfaces on top of it, which is the layered-stack pattern the chapter describes later.

The practical implication for designers is that interface categories are guides, not laws. Workloads such as logs and AI training data that once needed a file system might be served by an object API with file-like features. Chapter 3 covers object storage in depth, including how S3, GCS and Azure Blob are built.

quiz.q: What makes Google's Rapid Storage blur the line between file and object storage?
quiz.a: It adds file-like traits to an object store: sub-millisecond latency, unlimited appends and a hierarchical namespace, built on Colossus's stateful protocol.

title: Durability: will my bytes still exist? S3 aims for 11 nines
body: Durability answers one question: will my data still exist? It is about not losing bytes, and it is expressed as a probability of data loss per year. Amazon S3 is designed for "99.999999999%" durability, known as eleven nines. Durability is achieved through redundancy (replication or erasure coding), automatic repair, and placing copies across independent failure domains so no single event can destroy all of them.
deeper:
Durability is distinct from availability and consistency, and mixing them up leads to bad designs. Durable data may still be temporarily unreachable; the point is only that it has not been lost.

The chapter's back-of-envelope math shows how durability is estimated: with 3 replicas, a 1.57% annual failure rate per disk, independent failures and one-day repair, the annual loss probability per object comes out around 1.7 x 10^-10, almost ten nines. But that model lies, because real failures are correlated. Google found that failures often come in bursts tied to rack or multi-rack events, so placement across failure domains matters more than copy count.

That is why S3's high durability rests on placement as well as redundancy: S3 stores data across at least 3 availability zones by default for most storage classes. Chapter 10 returns to durability math, scrubbing, backups and multi-region design.

quiz.q: What does a durability figure like eleven nines actually measure?
quiz.a: The probability that stored data is not lost in a year, i.e. that bytes still exist, regardless of whether they can be reached at any given moment.

title: Availability: can I reach it now? Same durability, different uptime
body: Availability asks: can I read or write my data right now? It is separate from durability. S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability, while S3 One Zone-IA is designed for 99.5%. Both classes keep the same eleven-nines durability design. So the same data can be extremely unlikely to be lost, yet noticeably more likely to be temporarily unreachable, depending on how it is stored and served.
deeper:
The S3 example shows the two properties are tuned independently. One Zone-IA, as its name says, keeps data in a single availability zone, so a zone-level problem makes it unreachable even though the bytes are safe; Standard spreads data across at least 3 zones, so it stays reachable when one zone has trouble.

Availability is often hurt by short, transient events rather than permanent loss: a node rebooting, a top-of-rack switch failing, or an upgrade taking nodes offline for seconds to minutes. In a one-year Google study of cells with 1,000 to 7,000 nodes, less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted longer than 15 minutes.

The chapter's takeaway puts it sharply: you can have eleven nines of durability with only 99.5% availability. Google also found that replicating across multiple cells greatly improves availability, which is why multi-zone and multi-region placement protect both properties. The senior staff lens asks for a durability target and a latency target separately for this reason.

quiz.q: How can two storage classes have the same durability but different availability?
quiz.a: Durability is about not losing bytes; availability about reaching them now. Single-zone storage can keep bytes safe yet be unreachable during a zone outage, as with S3 One Zone-IA's 99.5%.

title: Consistency: will every later read see my write?
body: Consistency asks: after a write succeeds, will every later read see it? Strong consistency means yes, always. Eventual consistency means readers may see old data for a while before all copies catch up. Some relaxed models go further: the Google File System's record append could even show duplicate records. Consistency is a third property, independent of durability and availability, and each system picks the guarantee its users can tolerate.
deeper:
Consistency matters because distributed storage keeps multiple copies, and copies can briefly disagree. Strong consistency hides that disagreement from readers, usually at the cost of coordination. Weaker models are cheaper and more available but push complexity onto applications, which must tolerate stale reads or deduplicate records.

GFS's relaxed record append is a good example of a deliberate trade: readers may see duplicate records, so applications built on it must be able to detect or tolerate duplicates themselves.

In the running example, profiles need low latency and strong consistency for some fields, which points to a replicated database or key-value store with a cache. Messages need per-user ordering. Consistency guarantees are also one reason full POSIX file semantics are expensive to distribute: operations like atomic rename are strong consistency promises about the namespace.

The Azure storage paper referenced in this chapter is titled "a highly available cloud storage service with strong consistency", showing that both can be achieved together with careful design.

quiz.q: Why might a system choose eventual consistency over strong consistency?
quiz.a: Strong consistency requires coordination between copies, which costs latency and availability. Eventual or relaxed models are cheaper and faster, at the price of stale reads or duplicates.

title: Durable but unreachable, or reachable but fragile
body: Durability and availability can separate in both directions. Data can be durable but unavailable: a rack is powered off or its top-of-rack switch fails, but the disks are fine, so the bytes are safe yet nobody can reach them. Data can be available but not durable: a value accepted into one server's RAM cache but not yet written to disk can be read right now, but a power loss would erase it forever.
deeper:
These examples are the answers to one of the chapter's check-your-understanding questions, and they are worth internalizing because systems pick different points on this spectrum.

The durable-but-unavailable case explains why rebuilding immediately after a node goes silent is wasteful: the data is probably still there. Google's study found less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted longer than 15 minutes, so GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding data from a missing node.

The available-but-not-durable case is a common trap in write paths. Acknowledging a write as soon as it reaches memory makes the system fast, but until the data is persisted and replicated, a single crash loses it. This is why DRAM is used for caches and hot metadata, not as the only copy.

When reviewing a design, ask separately: what is the smallest event that makes this data unreachable, and what is the smallest event that makes it gone? Those are often different answers.

quiz.q: Give an example of data that is available but not durable.
quiz.a: A write accepted into a single server's RAM cache but not yet persisted to disk: readable now, but a power loss or crash would erase it.

title: Wait 15 minutes before rebuilding: most outages heal themselves
body: When a storage node disappears, should the system rebuild its data elsewhere immediately? Google studied storage cells of 1,000 to 7,000 nodes for one year and found that less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted longer than 15 minutes. So GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding data from a missing node. Rebuilding too early wastes network bandwidth and disk I/O copying data for nodes that will soon come back.
deeper:
The 15-minute wait is a trade-off between two risks. Wait too little, and routine events such as reboots, brief network blips or upgrades trigger massive repair traffic for data that was never lost. That traffic competes with user I/O and can itself slow the system down. Wait too long, and data sits with reduced redundancy, exposed to a second failure.

Upgrades are one source of these short absences. Azure notes that storage nodes go offline for seconds to minutes during upgrades, so a system that rebuilt instantly would treat every rolling deploy as a disaster.

The same idea appears in the durability math: the repair window is a key input. A one-day window makes the chance of a second failure during repair about 4.3 x 10^-5 per disk. The chosen delay therefore affects both efficiency and durability, and it should be based on measured outage durations, as Google's was.

quiz.q: Why did GFS wait 15 minutes before re-replicating a missing node's data?
quiz.a: Google found fewer than 10% of node outages lasted over 15 minutes; rebuilding sooner would waste network and disk copying data for nodes that come back.

title: 3x replication: simple, fast, and 200% overhead
body: Replication keeps N full copies of data on different machines. With 3x replication, any two copies can be lost and the data survives. The storage overhead is 3x, which is 200% extra space. Repair is cheap and simple: copy one surviving replica. Reads and writes are fast: any replica can serve a read, and a small write is just 3 I/Os. That makes replication great for hot data, despite its cost.
deeper:
Replication is the baseline every other scheme is measured against. In the chapter's comparison table, 3x replication uses 3 copies, 3.0x overhead, tolerates 2 losses, and needs to read only 1 fragment to repair a lost one.

Its strengths all come from each copy being complete. Repair reads one copy, so it generates little network traffic and finishes quickly, shrinking the window when data has reduced redundancy. Any replica can serve a read, spreading hot-read load. A write simply goes to three places, with no computation.

Its weakness is cost at scale. Storing each byte three times means 3 exabytes of raw disk per exabyte of user data, versus 1.33 exabytes with an efficient erasure code. HDFS illustrates the gap: a 6-block file takes 18 blocks with 3x replication but only 9 with RS(6,3), which also tolerates more failures.

This is why production systems use replication for new, hot or small data and switch to erasure coding once data is sealed and cooler.

quiz.q: Why is replication better than erasure coding for hot, frequently written data?
quiz.a: Any replica serves reads, small writes are just 3 I/Os, and repair copies a single replica, so latency and repair cost are low despite 3x overhead.

title: Erasure coding: any k of k+m fragments rebuild the data
body: Erasure coding (EC) splits data into k data fragments and computes m extra parity fragments. Any k of the k+m fragments can rebuild the original data, so up to m fragments can be lost. The most common family is Reed-Solomon, written RS(k, m) in this book; some papers write it the other way around, so always check. Storage overhead is (k + m) / k, far lower than full replication for similar or better fault tolerance.
deeper:
The chapter's comparison table makes the trade-offs concrete. RS(6,3) has 9 fragments, 1.5x overhead, tolerates 3 losses, and reads 6 fragments to repair one. RS(10,4) has 14 fragments, 1.4x overhead, tolerates 4 losses, and reads 10 to repair one. RS(12,4) has 16 fragments, 1.33x overhead, tolerates 4 losses, and reads 12 to repair one. Azure's LRC(12,2,2) also has 16 fragments and 1.33x, tolerates any 3 and many 4-failure patterns, and reads only 6 to repair one.

The HDFS example: a file of 6 blocks takes 18 blocks with 3x replication, but only 9 blocks with RS(6,3). That is half the disk and more failure tolerance, 3 losses instead of 2.

Worked example from the chapter's quiz: RS(10,4) has overhead (10+4)/10 = 1.4x, tolerates any 4 lost fragments, and a classic RS repair reads 10 fragments. Note the pattern: repair reads equal k, so wider codes save space but make each repair read more.

quiz.q: Compute RS(10,4)'s overhead, loss tolerance, and fragments read to repair one.
quiz.a: Overhead (10+4)/10 = 1.4x; it tolerates any 4 lost fragments; a classic Reed-Solomon repair reads k = 10 fragments.

title: Why not always erasure code? Repair traffic, small writes, slow reads
body: Erasure coding saves space but has three costs. Repair traffic: rebuilding one RS(6,3) fragment reads 6 fragments over the network, while replication reads just one copy. Small writes: RS(10,4) turns one small write into 14 I/Os instead of 3, because every fragment must be updated. Degraded reads: if a fragment is offline, the read must fetch k other fragments and reconstruct, waiting for the slowest of them.
deeper:
Each cost gets worse as codes get wider. Repair reads scale with k, so an RS(12,4) repair reads 12 fragments, raising both network traffic and the chance of hitting a slow or overloaded node. Slower repairs also lengthen the time a stripe stays degraded, exposed to further failures.

Small writes are the worst fit. Replication writes three copies; EC must touch all k+m fragments, which is why appending small records directly into an EC stripe is expensive.

Degraded reads hurt tail latency. A normal read might fetch just the fragment it needs. A degraded read waits for k fragments and the slowest of them determines latency, echoing the fan-out problem with SSD tails.

The flip side is that EC reconstruction can also rescue latency: Azure starts a parallel reconstruction when a fragment read looks slow and returns whichever finishes first.

The chapter's takeaway: EC cuts overhead from 3x to 1.33x to 1.5x, but costs more repair traffic, more I/Os for small writes, and worse degraded-read latency.

quiz.q: Why does erasure coding hurt small writes compared with replication?
quiz.a: A small write must update every fragment in the stripe, e.g. 14 I/Os for RS(10,4) versus 3 for 3x replication.

title: Write replicated, seal, then erasure code in the background
body: Production systems usually get the best of both schemes: write data replicated first, then erasure code it later. Azure's stream layer writes 3 replicas, seals an extent once it reaches about 1 GB, then erasure codes it lazily in the background and deletes the replicas afterwards. Meta's Tectonic blob storage does the same: replicated quorum appends for small writes, then re-encoding to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed.
deeper:
The reasoning follows from EC's costs. Small appends are cheap and fast with replication (3 I/Os) but expensive with EC (14 I/Os for RS(10,4)). While data is being written, it is also typically hottest, so replication's fast reads help too.

Sealing is the turning point. Once an extent or block is sealed, it is immutable, so there will be no more small updates to pay for. At that point one large encode is efficient, each fragment can be written sequentially to its target disk, and the replicas can be deleted to reclaim space.

The background, lazy nature also matters. Encoding is deferred work, so it can be scheduled when resources are available rather than on the write path, keeping user-facing latency low.

The running example follows the same pattern for photos and videos: replicated when new, erasure coded when warm. The chapter's takeaway sums it up: systems write replicated, then encode after sealing.

quiz.q: Why do Azure and Tectonic write replicated first and erasure code later?
quiz.a: Small appends cost 3 I/Os replicated but 14 with RS(10,4). After sealing, data is immutable, so one efficient bulk encode can run and the replicas get deleted.

title: Why Azure wasn't happy with RS(12,4)
body: Microsoft wanted a storage overhead of 1.33x for Azure. A standard Reed-Solomon code, RS(12,4), gives exactly that: 12 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, 16 in total. But repairing one lost fragment with RS(12,4) means reading 12 other fragments. Reading that many fragments raises the chance of hitting a slow or hot node, making repairs slower and more expensive. Microsoft's answer was a new code: Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC).
deeper:
The problem is the core trade-off of wide codes. Large k lowers overhead, but because a Reed-Solomon repair reads k fragments, every repair gets more network-heavy as k grows. More fragments also means more machines involved, and the slowest one determines when the repair finishes.

Repairs are not rare events at scale. With a 1.57% annual failure rate, a large fleet loses drives every day, and servers also go offline temporarily during upgrades. Each of those triggers reconstruction reads, both for permanent repair and for degraded reads that must serve data while a fragment is missing.

Compare the options from the chapter's table: RS(6,3) repairs with 6 reads but costs 1.5x overhead; RS(12,4) reaches 1.33x but needs 12 reads. Microsoft wanted the overhead of the second with the repair cost of the first. The motivation matters for Azure's business: Microsoft said erasure coding could cut storage cost by over 50% and its datacenter footprint by half.

quiz.q: What problem with RS(12,4) led Microsoft to design LRC?
quiz.a: RS(12,4) hits 1.33x overhead, but each single-fragment repair reads 12 fragments, adding network traffic and raising the chance of waiting on a slow or hot node.

title: LRC(12,2,2): two local groups of 6, plus 2 global parities
body: Azure's Local Reconstruction Code LRC(12,2,2) splits 12 data fragments into two local groups of 6. Each group gets one local parity fragment. Then 2 global parities are computed across all 12 data fragments. That makes 16 fragments in total, so overhead is 16/12 = 1.33x. A lost data fragment is rebuilt from its own local group: the other 5 data fragments plus the group's local parity, just 6 reads instead of 12.
deeper:
The design splits the two jobs of parity. Local parities make the common case cheap: most failures are single fragments, and those are fixed within a group of 6. Global parities provide protection against larger failures across the whole stripe.

In the chapter's table, LRC(12,2,2) has 16 fragments, 1.33x overhead, tolerates any 3 failures and many 4-failure patterns, and reads 6 fragments to repair one. RS(12,4), by comparison, tolerates any 4 but reads 12 for every repair.

Fragment placement still matters. Azure lays out LRC fragments across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains, so no single rack failure or rolling upgrade takes out too many fragments of one stripe.

This is the answer to one of the chapter's quiz questions: 12 data fragments in 2 local groups of 6, each with 1 local parity, plus 2 global parities, gives 16 fragments and 1.33x, and a single lost data fragment is rebuilt from 6 reads.

quiz.q: How does LRC(12,2,2) reach 1.33x overhead while needing only 6 reads for a single repair?
quiz.a: 16 fragments (12 data, 2 local, 2 global parity) over 12 data gives 1.33x; a lost fragment is rebuilt from its local group's other 5 data fragments plus local parity.

title: 0.17x less overhead = 170 PB of disk you never buy
body: Compared with RS(6,3), Azure's LRC(12,2,2) keeps the repair cost the same, 6 fragment reads, but cuts storage overhead from 1.5x to 1.33x. Microsoft says LRC is also more durable than keeping 3 replicas. The savings look small as a ratio, but at scale they are enormous: saving 0.17x of overhead on one exabyte of user data is 170 petabytes of disk you do not have to buy.
deeper:
LRC shows why storage engineers obsess over fractions of overhead. For every exabyte stored, the difference between 3x replication (3 exabytes of raw disk) and 1.33x (1.33 exabytes) is 1.67 exabytes. Even the smaller step from 1.5x to 1.33x is 170 petabytes per exabyte, with the servers, racks, power and space that go with it.

What makes LRC notable is that it did not trade away the thing that matters for hot data. The senior staff lens warns that wide codes save space but make repairs slower and more network-heavy. LRC reaches the overhead of a wide code while keeping repair reads at 6, the same as the narrower RS(6,3).

The claim that LRC is more durable than 3 replicas matters too: its fault tolerance (any 3 failures and many 4-failure patterns) exceeds replication's 2. Combined with placement across 20 fault domains, Azure got cheaper and more durable storage at once. The chapter's takeaway lists LRC as keeping 1.33x overhead while rebuilding from 6 reads instead of 12.

quiz.q: Why does going from 1.5x to 1.33x overhead matter so much?
quiz.a: At exabyte scale the 0.17x difference is 170 PB of disk per exabyte stored, plus servers, power and space, and LRC gets it without raising repair reads.

title: Pick the erasure code for the failure you fear most
body: Senior staff lens: the right erasure code depends on the failure you fear most. Wide codes, with a large number of data fragments k, save space but make repairs slower and more network-heavy, which increases the time a stripe stays degraded (missing a fragment and exposed to further losses). For hot data, the number of repair reads and degraded-read tail latency often matter more than squeezing out the last few percent of overhead.
deeper:
Framing the choice as a question about failure modes helps avoid optimizing the wrong metric. If you fear cost most, as with cold archive data, a wider code with lower overhead makes sense. If you fear slow reads during failures, as with hot data serving users, a narrower code or replication keeps repairs and degraded reads fast.

The mechanics behind this: repair reads equal k for Reed-Solomon, so RS(12,4) reads 12 fragments while RS(6,3) reads 6. More reads means more network traffic, a higher chance of hitting a slow or busy node, and a longer repair. During that time, the stripe has less margin before data loss.

Degraded reads face the same issue from the user's side: a read that must reconstruct waits for k fragments and the slowest of them.

This is why systems keep hot data replicated and encode once data is sealed and cooler, and why Azure invented LRC rather than simply adopting the widest code available.

quiz.q: Why might a team choose a narrower code with more overhead for hot data?
quiz.a: Narrow codes need fewer repair and degraded reads, so repairs finish faster and read tails stay low; for hot data that matters more than a few percent of space.

title: Ten nines on paper: back-of-envelope replica durability
body: You can estimate durability with simple math. Assume 3 replicas on 3 different disks, a 1.57% annual failure rate per disk (Backblaze 2024), independent failures, and one day to rebuild a lost replica. The chance of a first failure among 3 disks per year is about 0.047. Data is lost only if the other two disks also fail during repair windows, giving an annual loss probability per object of roughly 1.7 x 10^-10, almost ten nines.
deeper:
