The steps are worth following. The chance a given disk fails in a 1-day window is about 0.0157 / 365, or 4.3 x 10^-5. The chance of a first failure among the 3 disks in a year is about 3 x 0.0157, or 0.047.

To lose the data, the second disk must fail during the first repair window, and the third during the second window. That is about 2 x 4.3 x 10^-5 x 4.3 x 10^-5, or 3.7 x 10^-9. Multiply by the chance of a first failure: 0.047 x 3.7 x 10^-9 is about 1.7 x 10^-10 annual loss probability per object.

The math shows which levers matter. Faster repair shrinks the window and directly cuts loss probability. Lower failure rates help too. And adding copies multiplies in another tiny factor.

But the chapter titles this calculation "why it lies": the independence assumption is wrong in practice, so this number is an optimistic estimate of durability, not a real guarantee.

quiz.q: In the replica durability estimate, why does faster repair improve durability so much?
quiz.a: Loss requires the other disks to fail during the repair window; shrinking the window shrinks each of those small probabilities, which are multiplied together.

title: Why the durability math lies: failures come in bursts
body: The simple durability calculation assumes disks fail independently. They do not. Google found that a large fraction of failures happen in bursts, mostly tied to rack or multi-rack events, and concluded that accounting for correlated failures is the critical element of availability models. A single rack power event destroys all three replicas at once if they share the rack. Placement, not just copy count, decides real durability.
deeper:
Correlated failures break the math because the model multiplies small independent probabilities. If one event can take out all copies at once, the loss probability is roughly the probability of that one event, which is far larger than the product of three tiny numbers.

The chapter's quiz answer captures it: the independent model assumes disks fail independently, but in reality failures come in bursts tied to racks, power and software. Google's 2010 study found most large failure bursts are rack or multi-rack events, and that modeling correlated failures is the critical element.

Sources of correlation include shared racks, shared power feeds, a top-of-rack switch, a firmware bug that hits every drive of one model, and upgrades that take many nodes offline together.

The fix is to design placement around failure domains: spread copies or fragments across racks, power domains, zones and regions, so the smallest event that destroys all copies is very rare. The next section of the chapter is devoted to exactly this.

quiz.q: Why is the independent-failure durability model optimistic?
quiz.a: Real failures are correlated: rack, power, firmware and upgrade events can take out several copies at once. Google found most large failure bursts are rack or multi-rack events.

title: Failure domains: disk, host, rack, power, zone, region
body: A failure domain is a set of components that can fail together because they share something. They nest from small to large: a disk (media errors, head crash, firmware); a host (motherboard, network card, kernel, storage daemon); a rack (top-of-rack switch, rack power); a power domain (shared power feed or PDU); an availability zone or datacenter (power, cooling, network); and a region (natural disaster, regional control-plane bug).
deeper:
Each level is a bigger blast radius. Protecting against disk failure alone is easy: put copies on different disks. But if those disks share a host, a motherboard failure takes them all. If hosts share a rack, a top-of-rack switch failure hides them all. And so on up to regions, where a natural disaster or a regional control-plane bug can affect everything in the area.

The useful habit is to identify, for any piece of data, the smallest failure domain that contains all its copies. That domain's failure rate, not the disks', is your real exposure. The chapter's common mistake phrases it as a question: what is the smallest event that destroys all copies?

Not every failure domain is physical. Software can create correlated failures too: a firmware bug in one drive model, or a regional control-plane bug. Upgrades form their own domain, which is why Azure tracks upgrade domains alongside fault domains when placing erasure-coded fragments.

quiz.q: What makes a set of components a single failure domain?
quiz.a: They share something, such as a host, rack switch, power feed, datacenter or firmware, so one event can make them all fail together.

title: One host dies, 30 to 100 disks go with it
body: Correlated failures take out many components at once. A single host failure takes out all 30 to 100 of its disks together. A top-of-rack switch failure makes an entire rack unreachable, even if every disk inside is fine. A firmware bug can hit every drive of one model at the same time, anywhere in the fleet. These events are why counting copies is not enough: you must know what those copies share.
deeper:
These examples come from different layers of the failure-domain hierarchy, and each has a different character.

A host failure is large and immediate: a dense storage server can hold dozens of disks, so copies placed on different disks of the same host offer no protection against it. It also creates a big repair job, since every chunk on those disks may need rebuilding.

A top-of-rack switch failure is usually an availability event, not a durability one: the data is intact but unreachable. It is the chapter's example of data that is durable but unavailable. Still, if all replicas share that rack, the data is completely inaccessible until the switch is fixed.

Firmware bugs are the sneakiest, because they cross physical boundaries. Copies spread across racks and zones can still share a drive model. The same logic applies to software bugs in storage daemons or kernels.

These are the reasons Google concluded correlated failures are the critical element in availability models.

quiz.q: Why can a firmware bug defeat placement across racks and zones?
quiz.a: It is a correlated failure along a different axis: every drive of one model can fail together wherever it is, so copies must also avoid sharing a single failing model.

title: Rule 1: spread copies across failure domains
body: The first rule for surviving correlated failures is to spread copies or erasure-coded fragments across failure domains. Azure builds each rack as a separate fault domain with redundant networking and power, and lays out LRC fragments across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains. Meta's Tectonic survives host, rack and power-domain failures. HDFS wants RS(6,3) fragments spread across at least 3 racks, ideally 9 or more.
deeper:
The goal is to ensure that no single event takes out more fragments than the code can tolerate. For 3x replication, that means the three copies must sit in three separate domains at every level you care about. For erasure coding, it means no domain may hold more than m fragments of a stripe.

HDFS shows the gradient. RS(6,3) has 9 fragments and tolerates 3 losses. With 3 racks, each rack holds 3 fragments, so losing one rack is survivable but leaves no margin. With 9 or more racks, each fragment has its own rack and a rack failure costs only one fragment.

Azure goes further by treating racks as fault domains with redundant networking and power, and by tracking upgrade domains separately so that rolling upgrades never take down too many fragments of one stripe.

Wide codes make this harder: a 16-fragment stripe needs many independent domains, which is why Azure spreads LRC across 20 fault domains.

quiz.q: Why does HDFS prefer RS(6,3) spread across 9 or more racks rather than just 3?
quiz.a: With 3 racks each holds 3 fragments, so one rack failure uses all the code's tolerance; with 9+ racks each rack holds one fragment, leaving margin for further failures.

title: Rule 2: your own rolling upgrade is a failure domain
body: Upgrades are a failure domain too. Azure notes that storage nodes go offline for seconds to minutes during software upgrades. A rolling deploy that restarts too many nodes at once takes several copies or fragments of the same data offline together, creating a correlated failure you caused yourself. That is why Azure tracks upgrade domains as well as fault domains, and why deploys must be paced against how data is placed.
deeper:
Planned maintenance feels safe because nothing is broken, but to the storage system a node that is restarting looks exactly like a failed one. If enough nodes holding the same stripe restart together, reads for that data become degraded or unavailable, and a real hardware failure during the deploy could push it into data loss.

Azure's answer is to define upgrade domains and place LRC fragments across 10 of them, so upgrading one domain at a time never takes out more fragments than the code can tolerate.

This connects to the rebuild delay: Google found most node unavailability is short, so GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding data from a missing node. Upgrade restarts are exactly this kind of short absence. Rebuilding every time a node restarts would flood the network with pointless repair traffic.

Chapter 9 covers operations, upgrades and migrations in depth, including safe rollouts. The core lesson here: treat deploy tooling as part of your durability design, not an afterthought.

quiz.q: Why is a rolling upgrade considered a failure domain?
quiz.a: Restarting nodes are offline for seconds to minutes; restarting too many holding the same data at once is a correlated outage, just self-inflicted.

title: Rule 3: zones and regions cover the biggest disasters
body: The largest failure domains, datacenters, availability zones and regions, are covered by multi-zone and multi-region placement. Amazon S3 stores data across at least 3 availability zones by default for most storage classes. Google found that replicating data across multiple cells, its independent storage clusters, greatly improves availability. Spreading this widely protects against power, cooling and network failures in a whole datacenter, and against natural disasters or regional control-plane bugs.
deeper:
The trade-off with the biggest domains is distance. Zones in one region are close enough for relatively fast replication, but regions can be continents apart, and light takes real time to cross an ocean. So multi-region placement adds latency to any synchronous write and costs cross-region network bandwidth.

The S3 storage classes illustrate the payoff. S3 Standard spreads data across at least 3 zones and is designed for 99.99% availability. S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in one zone and is designed for 99.5% availability. Both share the eleven-nines durability design, but only the multi-zone class stays reachable through a zone outage.

Google's finding about multiple cells is the availability counterpart: a problem in one cell does not affect copies in another.

Chapter 10 covers reliability, durability and disaster recovery in more depth, including multi-region design and backups.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of multi-region placement, and what does it protect against?
quiz.a: It adds latency and cross-region bandwidth cost, because data must travel far; it protects against regional disasters and regional control-plane bugs.

title: Three replicas in one rack is really one replica
body: Common mistake: counting replicas without checking placement. "Three replicas" all in one rack are roughly one replica against a rack failure, because a single top-of-rack switch or rack power event takes all of them offline or destroys them together. The copy count looks safe on paper while the real protection is minimal. Always ask: what is the smallest event that destroys all copies of this data?
deeper:
This mistake is the practical form of the chapter's warning that the independent-failure durability math lies. The calculation assumed 3 replicas on 3 disks failing independently and produced almost ten nines. Put those disks in one rack and a single rack event, far more likely than three independent disk failures in a short window, loses everything.

The "smallest event" question works at every level. If all copies share a host, the smallest event is a motherboard failure. If they share a power feed, it is a PDU fault. If they share a region, it is a regional disaster or control-plane bug. If they share a drive model, it is a firmware bug.

The same logic applies to erasure coding: a 9-fragment RS(6,3) stripe across only 3 racks has 3 fragments per rack, so one rack failure consumes the code's entire tolerance.

The chapter's takeaway: correlated failures (rack, power, upgrades, firmware) dominate real durability, so placement across failure domains matters more than replica count.

quiz.q: Why are three replicas in one rack roughly one replica against a rack failure?
quiz.a: A single rack event (switch or power) hits all three at once, so the copies do not fail independently and give no more protection than one copy.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: Big companies build a stack of storage layers, not one system
body: Big companies do not build one storage system. They build a stack of layers, each solving one problem and exposing a simpler interface to the layer above. From bottom to top: hardware (HDD, SSD, network cards, racks, power); storage node software (chunk or extent servers); a distributed file system or storage layer (Colossus, Tectonic, HDFS, Azure stream layer); databases, key-value stores, object stores and data lake tables; and applications.
deeper:
The middle of the stack branches. On top of the storage layer sit databases and key-value stores (Spanner, Bigtable, ZippyDB, Cassandra, MySQL) and object and blob stores (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Ambry). Data lake tables (Iceberg, Hudi, Delta) are table formats built on files, sitting higher in the stack. Applications such as feed, messaging, search, ads and ML training use whichever service fits each data type.

The layering mirrors the running example: profiles go to a database, photos to a blob store, analytics to lake tables, but all of them ultimately rely on the same distributed storage layer for durability.

The benefit is that each hard problem is solved once. Replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing live in the storage layer, so a database team does not reimplement them. The cost is coupling: when the bottom layer has problems such as tail latency, every layer above feels them.

The rest of the book is organized roughly along this stack, from distributed file systems in Chapter 2 upward.

quiz.q: Why do big companies build storage as layers instead of one monolithic system?
quiz.a: Each layer solves one hard problem once, like durability in the storage layer, and exposes a simpler interface, so services above reuse it instead of rebuilding it.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: Bottom layers: hardware and storage node software
body: The two bottom layers of the storage stack are hardware and storage node software. Hardware (HDDs, SSDs, network cards, racks, power) is chosen for cost per TB, IOPS per TB, and power per TB. Storage node software runs on each server and stores chunks (in GFS and Tectonic) or extents (in Azure), either as files on a local file system or directly on the raw device. Tectonic nodes store chunks as files on XFS.
deeper:
The three hardware metrics map directly onto the chapter's earlier lessons. Cost per TB favors large HDDs, whose price fell from $0.114 per GB in 2009 to $0.014 in November 2022. IOPS per TB favors flash, because HDD random IOPS stay near 80 per drive while capacity grows. Power per TB matters because a large fleet's electricity and cooling are a major cost, which is one reason tape, which uses no power on a shelf, still has a role in archives.

Storage node software is deliberately simple. It knows about chunks or extents, blocks of data identified by ID, not about files, users or tables. Higher layers decide what the chunks mean and where replicas or fragments go.

The choice between a local file system and raw device is a trade-off. Storing chunks as files on XFS, as Tectonic does, reuses a mature file system. Writing directly to the raw device avoids a layer of overhead and gives full control, useful for things like aligning writes to host-managed SMR zones.

quiz.q: What three metrics drive hardware choice at the bottom of the storage stack?
quiz.a: Cost per TB, IOPS per TB and power per TB, balancing cheap capacity against enough random access and the running cost of electricity.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: The storage layer: turning thousands of nodes into one durable pool
body: The distributed file system or storage layer turns thousands of storage nodes into one durable pool with a namespace. It handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing so nothing above it has to. Google's Colossus underpins most Google Cloud products and is used by Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. Meta has Tectonic. Azure has the stream layer inside each storage stamp. HDFS plays this role in Hadoop deployments.
deeper:
This layer is where most of the chapter's durability machinery lives. It decides where replicas or fragments go across failure domains, notices when nodes disappear, waits an appropriate time (GFS used 15 minutes) before rebuilding, and moves data to balance load and capacity.

It is also where write-replicated-then-encode policies run. Azure's stream layer writes 3 replicas, seals an extent at about 1 GB, and then erasure codes it lazily with LRC. Tectonic uses replicated quorum appends for small writes and re-encodes to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed.

The namespace is the hard part. Chapter 2 argues that scaling metadata is the central problem of distributed file systems, and covers GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph and Lustre.

Because this layer is shared by everything above, its behavior shapes the whole company's storage. Colossus's SSD cache (L4) with machine-learning placement, for instance, can benefit the Google services that sit on top of it.

quiz.q: What responsibilities belong to the distributed storage layer in the stack?
quiz.a: Pooling many nodes into one durable namespace, plus replication, erasure coding, repair after failures and rebalancing, so higher layers get durability for free.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: Databases, object stores and lakes add semantics on top
body: Above the shared storage layer, databases, object stores and data lakes add semantics: transactions, indexes, key lookups and object APIs. They do not reimplement durability; they store their data in the layer below. Azure's partition layer, which serves Blobs, Tables and Queues, stores everything in the stream layer. At the very top, applications pick the right service for each data type, such as a database for profiles and a blob store for photos.
deeper:
This is where the variety of the running example gets served. Examples in the chapter's diagram include databases and key-value stores such as Spanner, Bigtable, ZippyDB, Cassandra and MySQL; object and blob stores such as S3, GCS, Azure Blob and Ambry; and data lake table formats such as Iceberg, Hudi and Delta, which sit on files.

The Google example makes the dependency clear: Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery all run on Colossus. Their teams focus on query processing, transactions and indexing while Colossus handles keeping bytes safe.

Applications like feed, messaging, search, ads and ML training sit on top and choose services per data type: profiles on a replicated database with cache, messages on an LSM-based database, photos on a blob store, logs through a log system like Kafka into a DFS or object store, analytics on lake tables.

Later chapters cover these services: object storage in Chapter 3, databases and storage engines in Chapter 5, caching in Chapter 6, and data lakes in Chapter 7.

quiz.q: Why doesn't a database built on Colossus need its own replication for durability?
quiz.a: The shared storage layer below already provides durability through replication and erasure coding; the database writes files to it and adds only its own semantics.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: Layering's deal: durability for free, tail latency for everyone
body: Why layer? Durability is hard and should be solved once. A database team writes files to the shared storage layer and gets durability for free, without building replication, erasure coding or repair itself. The cost is that problems in the bottom layer show up everywhere above. If the storage layer suffers tail latency spikes, every database, object store and application built on it inherits those spikes.
deeper:
The trade-off is shared infrastructure versus shared fate. Solving durability once saves enormous engineering effort and hardware: every team uses the same efficient erasure coding and placement logic, and the pool of disks is shared, so capacity and IOPS can be balanced across tenants.

But coupling means the bottom layer's weaknesses propagate. SSD garbage collection spikes, HDD IOPS limits, degraded reads during repair or slow nodes during upgrades all become latency that higher layers must absorb. Because a request at the top may fan out into many reads at the bottom, a small tail problem below can become a large one above.

This is why the senior staff lens repeatedly emphasizes designing for the tail, and why fixes for slow reads, like hedged reads or Azure's parallel reconstruction of slow fragments, are so valuable.

It also raises the stakes of operations: an upgrade or bug in the shared layer can affect every service at once, making it one of the largest failure domains.

quiz.q: What is the main downside of building all services on one shared storage layer?
quiz.a: Problems in the bottom layer, such as tail latency or outages, propagate to every service above it, so one layer's weakness becomes everyone's.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
title: Google, Microsoft, Meta all converged on one shared storage layer
body: In industry: Google (Colossus), Microsoft (the Azure stream layer, described in 2011) and Meta (Tectonic, described in 2021) converged on the same architecture: one shared storage layer with specialized services built on top. The payoff can be large. When Meta moved its data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic, it cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10x, because one pooled layer replaced many separate clusters.
deeper:
The convergence is a strong signal that the layered design is not a fashion but a response to the same pressures: failure is routine, durability is hard, and cost at exabyte scale rewards pooling.

The Meta example shows why pooling pays. Separate clusters per workload each need their own headroom, their own repair capacity and their own balance of IOPS and capacity. A shared layer like Tectonic can mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, using both resources efficiently instead of leaving one idle. Tectonic's blob storage also re-encodes sealed blocks to RS(10,4), about 1.4x overhead instead of 3x.

Colossus's scope shows the other side: it underpins most Google Cloud products, including Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery, and enables newer products like Rapid Storage, which offers sub-millisecond latency and a hierarchical namespace on top of Colossus's stateful protocol.

Chapter 13 goes company by company through how each assembled its stack, and why.

quiz.q: What did Meta gain by moving its data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic?
quiz.a: Consolidating onto a shared storage layer cut its number of warehouse clusters by 10x, pooling capacity and IOPS instead of running many separate clusters.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
title: Profiles and messages: small records, opposite access patterns
body: Profiles are small records, billions of them, and read-heavy. They need low latency and strong consistency for some fields, so they fit a replicated database or key-value store plus a cache, on SSD with a DRAM cache (Chapters 5 and 6). Messages are also small records, but write-heavy. They need high write throughput and per-user ordering, so they fit a log-structured (LSM) database on SSD (Chapter 5).
deeper:
Both types are small, hot and mutable, which is why both land on flash with replication. The difference is the read/write balance.

Profiles are read far more than written, so a DRAM cache absorbs most reads and the database behind it provides durability and consistency. Some fields, such as settings, may need strong consistency so a user sees their own changes immediately; others can tolerate brief staleness.

Messages flip the pattern: they are written constantly. An LSM (log-structured merge) database turns many small writes into large sequential ones, which suits flash, where large sequential writes give the lowest write amplification and the least wear. Per-user ordering matters because a conversation must display in sequence.

Neither belongs on HDD: their random access patterns would quickly exhaust an HDD's roughly 80 IOPS, the IOPS-per-TB problem that made Haystack IOPS-bound. Chapter 5 compares B-trees and LSM-trees and covers RocksDB and sharded databases, and Chapter 6 covers caching tiers.

quiz.q: Why does the running example put messages on an LSM database rather than a read-optimized store?
quiz.a: Messages are small and write-heavy; an LSM design turns many small writes into sequential ones, giving the high write throughput needed, on SSD.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
title: Photos, logs, analytics, backups: big data, cheap media
body: The large-data types map to cheaper media. Photos and videos are write-once blobs, hot then cold: an object or blob store, replicated when new and erasure coded when warm, on HDD with SSD cache and a CDN. Logs and events are append-only and huge: a log system like Kafka landing in a DFS or object store. Analytics and ML data is columnar and scanned: a data lake. Backups go to an archive tier or tape.
deeper:
More detail per type, from the chapter's mapping table. Photos and videos need cheap durability, high throughput and a CDN (Chapters 3 and 7). Logs and events need append throughput and cheap retention, using SSD for hot data and HDD for bulk (Chapters 2, 3 and 7). Analytics and ML data needs aggregate throughput, low cost and table formats; it lives in a data lake on an object store or DFS, on HDD bulk with SSD or NVMe caching for training (Chapters 2 and 7). Backups and compliance archives are rarely read but must be kept for years; they need lowest cost and immutability, on an archive object tier or tape with an HDD cold tier (Chapters 7 and 11).

All four share traits that suit HDD and erasure coding: large size, mostly immutable data, and sequential access. Photos show the lifecycle pattern: replicated while new and hot, then erasure coded once they cool, matching the write-replicated-then-encode approach Azure and Tectonic use.

Together with profiles and messages (SSD, replicated), this is the chapter's quiz answer for the five running-example data types.

quiz.q: Why are photos replicated when new but erasure coded when warm?
quiz.a: New photos are hot and freshly written, where replication gives cheap writes and fast reads; once they cool and are immutable, erasure coding cuts storage cost.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
title: The whole pattern: hot on flash replicated, cold on HDD erasure coded
body: The running example reveals one pattern. Small, hot, mutable data lives on flash with replication: profiles and messages. Large, cold, immutable data lives on hard disks with erasure coding: aged photos and videos, logs, analytics files and backups. The layers in between, caches, databases, object stores, lakes and tiering, exist to move data between those two worlds as it is written, read, cools down and ages.
deeper:
Each half of the pattern follows from earlier lessons. Hot data needs IOPS and low latency, and HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling, so flash wins. Hot data is also written and read often, where replication's cheap small writes (3 I/Os), fast repairs and any-replica reads beat erasure coding's 14 I/Os per small write for RS(10,4).

Cold data needs cheap capacity, and HDDs at $0.014 per GB (Backblaze, November 2022) with large sequential I/O deliver it. Cold data is immutable, so erasure coding's weaknesses (small writes, repair traffic) matter less, and its 1.33x to 1.5x overhead versus 3x saves huge amounts of disk.

The transitions are where engineering effort goes: sealing extents and encoding them in the background, caching hot items in DRAM or SSD, and tiering data down to archive or tape as it ages. Chapter 7 covers hot, warm and cold tiers, lifecycle policies and tape; Chapter 12 covers the cost side, including media mix and utilization.

quiz.q: Why does cold, immutable data suit erasure coding better than hot, mutable data?
quiz.a: EC's costs hit small writes, repairs and degraded reads, which cold data rarely triggers; its lower overhead then saves large amounts of disk.

section: Map of the rest of the book
title: Where the book goes next: 13 chapters on one storage stack
body: The rest of the book builds on this chapter. Chapter 2: distributed file systems, with metadata scaling as the theme. Chapter 3: object storage. Chapter 4: block, local and Kubernetes storage. Chapter 5: databases and storage engines. Chapter 6: caching tiers. Chapter 7: data lakes, tiering and archival. Chapter 8: scaling. Chapter 9: operations, upgrades and migrations. Chapter 10: reliability and disaster recovery. Chapters 11 to 14: compliance, cost, company case studies, and the senior staff lens.
deeper:
More detail on what each chapter covers. Chapter 2 covers GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph and Lustre. Chapter 3 explains how S3, GCS and Azure Blob are built. Chapter 4 covers network block devices, local NVMe, CSI and persistent volumes. Chapter 5 compares B-trees and LSM-trees, RocksDB and sharded databases. Chapter 6 covers DRAM and flash caches, hot keys, and caches as a reliability risk. Chapter 7 covers hot, warm and cold tiers, lifecycle and tape. Chapter 8 covers sharding, rebalancing, hot spots and capacity planning. Chapter 9 covers safe rollouts and moving exabytes. Chapter 10 covers durability math, scrubbing, backups and multi-region. Chapter 11 covers encryption, keys, deletion and residency. Chapter 12 covers cost per useful byte, media mix and utilization. Chapter 13 walks through how each big company assembled its stack, and why. Chapter 14 covers leading storage design reviews and making long-term bets.

The order roughly follows the layered stack: storage layer first, then services on top, then cross-cutting concerns like operations, reliability, security and cost.

quiz.q: Which chapter tackles the metadata scaling problem introduced in Chapter 1?
quiz.a: Chapter 2, on distributed file systems (GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph, Lustre), whose central theme is scaling metadata.

title: Chapter 1 recap: failure, physics, and cost shape everything
body: Chapter 1's key takeaways: at big-tech scale failure is routine, about 13 drives a day from 300,000 drives at 1.57% AFR, so repair must be automatic. Media latency spans about six orders of magnitude, from DRAM (~100 ns) to HDD (~10 ms) to tape. SSDs cannot overwrite in place, which explains their wear and tail spikes. HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling, pushing hot data to flash.
deeper:
The remaining takeaways. Block, file and object are three interfaces with different semantics: object dominates large, immutable data; block dominates databases and VMs; file dominates HPC, AI training and legacy big data. Durability, availability and consistency are different properties: you can have eleven nines of durability with only 99.5% availability.

Erasure coding cuts overhead from 3x to 1.33x to 1.5x, but costs more repair traffic, more I/Os for small writes and worse degraded-read latency, so systems write replicated and encode after sealing. Azure's LRC(12,2,2) keeps 1.33x overhead but rebuilds a lost fragment from 6 reads instead of 12.

Correlated failures (rack, power, upgrades, firmware) dominate real durability, so placement across failure domains matters more than replica count. And big companies build one shared storage layer (Colossus, Tectonic, Azure stream layer) with databases, object stores and lakes on top.

The unifying idea: storage design is driven by failure, physics and cost, and the senior staff lens's four questions (access pattern, durability, latency including tail, cost per useful byte) test all three.

quiz.q: Why must repair be automatic in a 300,000-drive fleet?
quiz.a: At 1.57% AFR about 13 drives die daily; manual handling cannot keep up, and delays leave data with reduced redundancy.
